power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Factor Structure of the Auditory-Visual Abnormalities Questionnaire and Development of a Brief Scale

text.text: Nikitova and colleagues' Auditory and Visual Abnormalities Questionnaire (AVAQ) is the first comprehensive assessment of the type of perceptual abnormalities associated with the schizophrenia spectrum (Nikitova et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Nikitova and colleagues' Auditory and Visual Abnormalities Questionnaire (AVAQ) is the first comprehensive assessment of the type of perceptual abnormalities associated with the schizophrenia spectrum <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Nikitova et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The primary aim of this study was to investigate the factor structure of the AVAQ and develop a brief version of the scale.

Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses indicated that the AVAQ is multidimensional, capturing a general factor of perceptual abnormalities, along with more specific types of perceptual abnormalities.
Through item-level analyses, we identified 23 items that capture this factor structure.
A Brief AVAQ scale consisting of these 23 items exhibited good reliability and convergent validity in two relatively large samples.
This scale could be used in both research and clinical practice.

Schizophrenia spectrum disorders (heretofore, schizophrenia) are severe mental illnesses characterized in part by perceptions and beliefs that do not conform to consensus reality: hallucinations and delusions, respectively.
Together, these symptoms comprise the psychotic symptoms of schizophrenia.
Hallucinations are defined as perceptions in the absence of corresponding sensory input.

They have a lifetime occurrence in over two thirds of individuals with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (McCarthy-Jones et al. 2017; Clark et al. 2017; Lim et al. 2016) and are often associated with profound distress.
text.formatted: They have a lifetime occurrence in over two thirds of individuals with schizophrenia spectrum disorders <ref type="bibr">(McCarthy-Jones et al. 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Clark et al. 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Lim et al. 2016)</ref> and are often associated with profound distress.

text.text: Alongside, and often preceding, full-blown hallucinations are perceptual anomalies, examples of which include altered perception of light or color intensity or distortions of sound.

These perceptual anomalies can be observed along the full psychosis spectrum (Silverstein & Lai 2021; Kelleher & Cannon 2010)-from individuals with mild, transient alterations in perception and belief (van Os et al. 2008) to those with psychotic illness.
text.formatted: These perceptual anomalies can be observed along the full psychosis spectrum <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Silverstein & Lai 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kelleher & Cannon 2010</ref>)-from individuals with mild, transient alterations in perception and belief <ref type="bibr">(van Os et al. 2008)</ref> to those with psychotic illness.

text.text: Critically, perceptual anomalies are associated with important clinical outcomes, such as depressive symptoms, suicidality, lower quality of life, worse functional outcomes, earlier age of schizophrenia onset, and increased delusions and hallucinations (Keane et al. 2018; Schwarzer et al. 2022; Granö et al. 2015).

text.text: Perceptual anomalies also have high sensitivity and specificity for predicting conversion to a psychotic disorder (Klosterkötter et al. 2001; Ciarleglio et al. 2018).

text.text: Thus, they show promise as prognostic indicators.

Abnormal perceptual experiences have historically been measured using clinical interviews that assess the so-called basic symptoms (i.e., the Bonn Scale, Huber & Gross 1989; the Frankfurt Complaint Questionnaire, Süllwold & Huber 1986): subtle, subjectively experienced disruptions in perception, thought, action, and emotions that are associated with the psychosis prodrome.

text.text: Their semi-structured format allows interviewers to clarify experiences that may be difficult to articulate and ask follow-up questions to distinguish basic symptoms from related phenomena, including frank psychotic symptoms.
Thus, these interviews are the gold standard measures for in-depth phenomenological characterization.
However, their length, reliance on specialized interviewer training, and associated participant and staff burden can limit their use, particularly for routine screening.

The Auditory and Visual Abnormalities Questionnaire (AVAQ) was developed as a psychometrically robust self-report measure designed to address the limitations of clinical interview measures of subjective perceptual anomalies (Nikitova et al., 2019).

text.text: These items were drawn from the phenomenological and experimental literature, and from established clinical interviews, including the Bonn Scale for the Assessment of Basic Symptoms.

Creation of a short from questionnaire requires an understanding how the full item pool is organized and any inter-item redundancy that can be removed without reducing the validity of the latent construct.

The current study therefore had three goals: 1) to evaluate the factor structure and item properties of the AVAQ in independent samples, 2) to use these findings to develop a brief version, and 3) to determine whether the brief version retains adequate reliability, content coverage, and external validity.
Together, these analyses assessed whether a reduced item set could efficiently capture the relevant range of auditory and visual distortions.

Nikitova et al.
reported that most items loaded strongly on the first component and on one additional component.
They concluded that a single component underlies AVAQ items and that the scale is therefore unidimensional.
However, this pattern suggests another possibility-the presence of a broad dimension common to many items along with specific dimensions associated with subsets of items.

That is, an item's loading on the first component would suggest variance shared with many other items, whereas its loading on a subsequent component would suggest additional (residual) variance shared primarily with a subset of conceptually related items (e.g., visual items).
Thus, the loading pattern that Nikitova et al. (2019) is consistent with a multidimensional structure that includes both general and specific sources of variance in perceptual abnormalities.

text.text: First, principal components analysis (PCA) and exploratory factor analysis (EFA) are distinct statistical techniques that serve different purposes (Fabrigar et al., 1999).
text.formatted: First, principal components analysis (PCA) and exploratory factor analysis (EFA) are distinct statistical techniques that serve different purposes <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Fabrigar et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: PCA is a data-reduction procedure that transforms a set of observed variables into a smaller set of components that account for maximal variance in the data.
In contrast, EFA is a latent-variable technique which postulates that common variance among observed variables arises from underlying latent variables (i.e., common factors).
Although PCA and EFA may sometimes yield similar results, they may yield materially different results.
Moreover, because EFA explicitly models latent variables, it is generally more informative than PCA for assessing the dimensionality of psychological scales (Fabrigar et al., 1999).

text.text: However, as Fabrigar et al. (1999) emphasized, both theory and empirical evidence suggest that psychological constructs are often correlated, making this assumption difficult to justify in most cases.

text.text: Accordingly, the primary aim of the present research was to re-examine the latent structure of the scale using factor-analytic methods (rather than PCA).
A second aim was to develop a brief version of the AVAQ for both research and clinical applications.
To achieve these aims, we administered the AVAQ and the SPQ to two independent samples.
Using a development sample, we conducted exploratory factor analyses (EFAs) to identify the latent structure of the AVAQ and to select items for a shortened form of the measure.
We then evaluated the replicability of the factor structure in an independent replication sample using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA).

Participants who consented to participate completed the demographic and background questionnaire.

We note two limitations of the present research.
The first is that the studies included only university students, limiting the generalizability of the results.
A specific concern is that there was a restricted range of sensory-perceptual abnormalities.
Sensory-perceptual abnormalities may lead to significant impairments in a person's ability to function in everyday environments, including the classroom.
Consequently, it seems likely that people who experience sensory-perceptual abnormalities on a frequent basis are underrepresented in university samples.

Restriction of range may simply attenuate factor loadings and correlations of AVAQ scores with other variables, but it is at least possible that a different factor structure would emerge in samples more representative of the general population and/or clinical samples.
The second limitation is that we collected only limited information relevant to the validity of the AVAQ.
The finding that Brief AVAQ scores correlated strongly with SPQ scores provides additional evidence for the construct validity of the AVAQ.
However, this evidence does not establish that the Brief AVAQ has predictive validity-in other words, that it correlates meaningfully with future outcomes.

Predictive validity could be investigated by including the AVAQ in longitudinal studies and determine whether people who report experiencing high levels of sensory-perceptual abnormalities are more likely to develop schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
Another issue for future research concerns the origin of the factors that emerged in the factor analyses.

The factors could represent continuous dimensions of variation in sensoryperceptual experience on which people differ (in the same way that, for example, the "big five" personality traits are continuous dimensions of variation in people's stable pattern of thinking, feeling, and behaving).
However, factors could also reflect subgroups of participants with distinctive profiles of sensory-perceptual abnormalities.

For example, the Auditory factor could be driven by a subgroup of participants who experience auditory abnormalities at a relatively high rate but are not prone to experience other types of abnormalities.
This issue could be investigated using cluster analysis.
Perceptual abnormalities are an important early warning sign of schizophrenia.
Here, using Nikitova et al.'s (2019) AVAQ, we investigated the factor structure of this psychological phenomenon.

In the present study, we show that the AVAQ can be reduced substantially-from 80 substantive items to 23-while preserving meaningful variation in sensory-perceptual experiences.
Factor analyses indicated that the AVAQ is multidimensional.
Seven interpretable factors emerged in an EFA performed on the development sample (Study 1).
We interpreted the first factor as a general factor, given that both auditory and visual items of various types loaded on this factor.

The second factor we interpreted as an auditory factor, and the remaining factors as types of visual abnormality: STM/attention, object perception, object distortion, face/body, and light sensitivity.
These findings clarify the structure of the experiences assessed by the AVAQ and provide a more efficient tool for studying them.
Based on factor loadings, we identified 23 items that captured the 7-factor structure of the AVAQ.
In a CFA, we specified a 7-factor measurement model, with these 23 items as indicators.
This structure provided an acceptable fit to the data in the replication sample (Study 2).
A hierarchical CFA indicated that the first factor reflects a general factor of perceptual abnormalities, whereas the other factors reflect more specific subtypes.

Even after looking at something for a while, I realize that there is a lot more there that I had not noticed

bib.title: The world looks like it is flat to me; completely lacking in depth
Objects appear to be too bright
It is hard to determine the shape of an object; I need to actually pick it up or look at it from different angles
When looking in the mirror, I know it is my face, but for some reason, my facial features look deformed
I see flashes of bright light, stars, flames, or spots of varying shapes
Words and sentences sound broken up or disconnected
I can only see parts of an object
Other people seem to have oddly shaped bodies
Everything I see is tinted in a certain color
When I hear something, I cannot tell where it is coming from, even though others can do so
In my head, I hear sounds like cracking, clapping, humming, banging, whistling, hissing, or knocking, but I know they are not really there
Objects appear to move, as if there were a very mild earthquake that slightly shook everything back and forth
Things can appear lopsided, with one side bigger and one side smaller than they really are
